title: The magic cost of fermionic randomness
authors: Chenfeng Cao, Yifan Tang, Jens Eisert
abstract: Sampling-based quantum advantage raises a basic resource question: how much non-Gaussianity is needed to reproduce the random-matrix statistics often associated with quantum chaos? Passive fermionic linear optics preserves Gaussian structure, and even Haar-random mode mixing fails to anticoncentrate for Slater inputs. We show that overcoming this obstruction requires an extensive input resource. For any pure half-filled input state, the one-body defect $ν$, defined as the summed occupation variance of the natural orbitals, must scale linearly with system size. For products of bounded-size blocks on $4N$ modes, this condition is also sufficient, with normalized collision moment asymptotic to $2N/ν$, compared with the Porter-Thomas value 2. For four-mode products, the full Porter-Thomas moment hierarchy is recovered precisely when the defect density tends to its maximum. Assuming average-case hardness, approximate classical sampling remains hard near maximal density, with an error tolerance that increases with the density. Two-copy number fluctuations measure $ν$ directly, and the same quantity lower-bounds the combined cost of non-Gaussian resource modes and parity-preserving local gates in deterministic exact preparation. Fermionic randomness therefore carries an extensive magic cost, with a quantitative link between sampling statistics, preparation resources, and an experimentally accessible witness.
summary:
This work quantifies the 'magic cost' of fermionic randomness, determining that achieving quantum chaotic sampling statistics requires the input state to possess a defect ($
u$) that scales linearly with system size. The authors establish a direct, measurable link between this defect and the necessary preparation resources, providing a quantitative witness for non-Gaussianity in fermionic quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper investigates the minimum non-Gaussian resource required in the input state of fermionic systems to achieve quantum sampling statistics associated with quantum chaos, especially when the evolution dynamics are passive and Gaussian.
main_result:
Achieving anticoncentration or approaching Porter-Thomas statistics requires the one-body defect ($
u$) to scale linearly with system size ($
u = \Omega(N)$), establishing an extensive 'magic cost' for fermionic randomness.
method: The analysis uses theoretical bounds derived from analyzing collision moments, two-copy interference protocols, and comparing asymptotic behavior to known random matrix statistics.
model_or_system:
The system models fermionic particles evolving via passive fermionic linear optics (FLO) on $2N$ fermions, analyzed specifically at half-filling. The resource is quantified by the one-body defect ($
u$).
key_observables:
One-body defect ($
u$), defect density ($\gamma$), normalized collision moment ($C_N$), and the two-copy variance ($	ext{Var}(\Delta n)$).
important_parameters: System size ($N$), defect density ($\gamma$), and the ratio of the collision moment to the Porter-Thomas value (2).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the evolution is passive and that the resource is entirely contained within the input state. Hardness results rely on conjectures regarding the polynomial hierarchy.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the relationship between the collision moment ($C_N$) and defect density ($\gamma$), showing the distinct asymptotic limits for Slater inputs versus the Porter-Thomas regime, and visualizing the two-copy variance measurement.
paper_structure:
The paper progresses by first establishing the obstruction caused by Gaussian evolution, then deriving the necessary scaling of the defect ($
u$) to overcome it, and finally providing a quantitative link between this defect and the preparation cost via two-copy measurements.
why_interesting:
It provides a rigorous, quantitative measure ($
u$) linking fundamental quantum resource limitations (non-Gaussianity) to observable statistical properties (collision moments) in fermionic many-body systems, which is highly relevant for understanding quantum simulation feasibility.
